narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily against your application were your class ranking in the third year of law school, your first-year class ranking, and your family income bracket. All three pushed the model toward predicting failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the fourth decile—noticeably lower than the average of accepted students. This was the strongest single reason the model expected you to struggle on the bar. Your first-year ranking was also below the typical accepted student, adding further concern. Finally, coming from an upper-middle-income family worked against you; while many accepted students share this background, the model learned that this group as a whole has a slightly higher risk of not passing on the first try.

Your LSAT and undergraduate GPA were only slightly below the averages of accepted applicants and played only a minor role. Gender and race were not factors in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance if you retake courses or consider programs that offer targeted bar-prep support. Raising your class standing and gaining additional structured study time could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor.
